To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
synaptically activated Ca waves and NMDa spikes locally suppress subsequent voltage‐dependent Ca signals in dendrites.
regenerative [Ca2+] changes caused by either Ca2+ waves or NMDA spikes suppress bAP‐evoced [Ca2+] increases.
regenerative [Ca2+] signals can suppress subsequent voltage‐dependent Ca 2+ signals in the same dendrites.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding how the location and magnitude of synaptically evoked [Ca2+]-changes in dendrites of pyramidal neurons are controlled and modulated by other Ca2+‐evoked changes in the same dendrite.
how Ca2+ signalling is regulated in dendrites of pyramidal cells.

how the spatial distribution of Ca2+ changes, caused by synaptic inputs or regenerative Ca2+, affects subsequent bAP‐mediated Ca2+ signalling, which in turn affects synaptic plasticity and dendritic gene expression.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the results demonstrate a novel form of dendritic Ca2+ signalling, where synaptically evoked Ca2+ signals locally suppress subsequent Ca2+ signals evoked by backpropagating action potentials.
synaptically evoked [Ca2+ ]i increases in pyramidal cells are locally regulated by Ca2+‐independent and Ca2+‐ dependent mechanisms that can suppress subsequent bAP‐dependent Ca2+.
the Ca2+ signals evoked by regenerative Ca release or NMDA spikes can suppress the subsequent bAP‐induced Ca signals in the same dendritic region.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
large [Ca2+‐]i changes locally suppress subsequent bAP‐induced [Ca2+]i signals, and that this is mediated by Ca2+‐independent inhibition of voltage‐gated channels.
synaptically activated [Ca2+] changes locally suppress bAP‐evolved [Ca2+] signalling in pyramidal cell apical dendrites.
Ca2+ waves or NMDA spikes can suppress bAP‐evolved [Ca2+] changes in pyramidal cell distal dendrites.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the magnitude and location of [Ca2+] increases, induced by regenerative Ca++ release and entry, locally modulate the magnitude of subsequent bAP‐induced [Ca2+] changes in pyramidal cell apical dendrites.
the large Ca2+ signals that occur at the synapse can locally suppress bAP signals.
the magnitude and time course, as well as location, of [Ca2+] changes in dendrites can be modulated by the preceding synaptic activity.
